title: The father who went to learn from a king
word: a teaching role in the house
hook: a son comes home stung, and his father says: I don't know either
carry: conduct here shapes the next birth
tomorrow: after all that teaching, what does Krishna tell Arjuna to do?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Upakosala's teacher was away, and the fires he tended taught him: Brahman is joy, as wide as space. Today, a father with no answer.
screen: `THE FIRES TAUGHT HIM.` · `TODAY: A QUESTION WITH NO ANSWER.`

segments.voice: A kid asks a question at bedtime, and the grown-up's mind goes blank. There's a quick way out: say something confident and change the subject. The Chandogya Upanishad has that moment. A young man, Shvetaketu, comes home stung. At a king's assembly he was asked questions about where people go when they leave this world, and he couldn't answer one. You told me you'd taught me everything, he says to his father. What does his father say?
screen: `A BEDTIME QUESTION.` → `A SON COMES HOME STUNG.` → `YOU SAID YOU'D TAUGHT ME.`

segments.voice: His father, Gautama, doesn't defend himself. You know me, he says. Whatever I knew, I told you. I don't know even one of these. Then he does something harder. He goes to the king, Pravahana Jaivali. The king offers him worldly wealth. Gautama turns it down: keep that; tell me what you said to my son. The king is uneasy. This knowledge, he says, has never gone to a brahmin before you. And a priest and father sits down to learn from a warrior king. The king answers the son's question: where do we go after this life? He calls it the five fires. Heaven, the rain cloud, the earth, a man, a woman: offered through each in turn, life comes down as rain, becomes food, then a child, and is born again. And there are two roads out of this world. Those who know this, and live in the forest with faith and discipline, go by the path of the gods, and don't come back. Those who live by rites, good works and giving go by the path of the ancestors, and return. Then the line that would shape the whole tradition: those whose conduct here has been good soon enter a good birth; those whose conduct has been foul, a foul one. Scholars count this among the earliest places a Hindu text spells out karma and rebirth: how you live shapes where you're born next. And it reached the tradition because a father admitted he didn't know, and walked out the door to learn it. It still sits under how Hindu families talk about life and death: what you do now carries forward. And when a child asks what happens when we die, Gautama shows the way: say what you know, admit what you don’t, and go learn.
screen: `I DON'T KNOW EVEN ONE.` · `KEEP THE WEALTH; TEACH ME.` · `THE FIVE FIRES, THE TWO PATHS.` · `CONDUCT SHAPES THE NEXT BIRTH.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and bring up one question you can’t answer yet, about life, death, or someone you love. Hold it lightly with the breath and let it stay unanswered. If you pray, you can offer the question just as it is; if not, let it sit beside you like a guest.
A teaching role in the house: in the Chandogya, a father admits he doesn't know, and goes out to learn.

howItsDone: Hindus still speak of karma and rebirth, and many families pass the teaching on at home: questions about God and death go from child to parent to grandparent, and sometimes on to a priest or teacher. Saying 'let's find out' is part of how it's handed down.

original.note: Sanskrit: Shvetaketu, the son who comes home stung; his father is Gautama (Uddalaka Aruni).

trapdoor: what you thought: karma and rebirth were always just there in Hinduism.
what it means: in the Chandogya, a king teaches it to a father who admitted he didn't know.

what a scholar hears: Chandogya 5.3–5.10, Pravahana Jaivali's five fires (panchagni-vidya), the path of the gods and the path of the fathers, and 5.10.7 on conduct and birth; the Brihadaranyaka tells the same scene at 6.2.

Shvetaketu.meaning: a young man who can't answer a king's questions

Gautama.meaning: Shvetaketu's father, who admits he doesn't know

Chandogya.meaning: an Upanishad full of stories of teachers and students

Pravahana Jaivali.meaning: the king who teaches Gautama the five fires

karma.meaning: action, and the way it shapes what comes next

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 5.3.1–5.3.5 (Shvetaketu at the Panchala assembly; the king's questions; he goes home: you said you had taught me; Gautama: whatever I knew I told you; I do not know even one of these)

Chandogya Upanishad 5.3.6–5.3.7 (Gautama goes to the king; refuses human wealth and asks for the words spoken to his son; the king, troubled, asks him to stay; this knowledge has not gone to brahmins before you; then he teaches him)

Chandogya Upanishad 5.4–5.10 (the five fires: yonder world, rain cloud, earth, man, woman, through which come soma, rain, food, seed and the child; those who know this and worship with faith and austerity in the forest go by the path of the gods and do not return; those who sacrifice, do public works and give in the village go by the path of the fathers and return; 5.10.7: those of pleasant conduct soon enter a pleasant womb, those of foul conduct a foul one)
